```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)

# Screenshots live in vignettes/images (excluded from the package build to keep
# it small) and are read from GitHub when the images are not available locally
screenshot <- function(file) {
  path <- file.path("images", file)
  if (!file.exists(path)) {
    path <- paste0(
      "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DillonHammill/DataEditR/master/",
      "vignettes/images/", file
    )
  }
  knitr::include_graphics(path)
}
```

**DataEditR** is an R package that makes it easy to interactively view, enter, filter and edit data. The data editor is a shiny application built on the MIT-licensed [Tabulator](https://tabulator.info) JavaScript library, so it stays fast with large datasets, and it can edit tables stored in a database as well as data in your R session. In this vignette we will explore the key features that are available through the `data_edit()` function.

## Preparation

In order to get started with **DataEditR**, we will need to install the package from CRAN and load it into our current R session:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
install.packages("DataEditR")
library(DataEditR)
```

If you would like to use the development version of **DataEditR** it can be installed directly from GitHub:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
devtools::install_github("DillonHammill/DataEditR")
```

## 1. Data Visualisation

Simply supply your data in the form of a matrix, data.frame, tibble or data.table to `data_edit()` to view it in an interactive table. For example, if we wanted to take a look at the `mtcars` dataset:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("editor.png")
```

The data editor has four parts:

* the **header** with the *Cancel* button, the name and size of the data, and the *Done* button. Click the name to rename the data: the code then gives the result the new name (`cars <- mtcars %>% ...`) and exported files are named after it;
* the **toolbar** to open other data, undo and redo changes, show or hide the column summaries (`Summaries`), select the columns to show (`Select`), filter rows (`Filters`, with the active filters next to it), see a row as a form (`Form`), review changes (`Review`), see the code that reproduces your edits (`Code`), export the data and see the keyboard shortcuts;
* the **grid**, which shows the row indices on the left (with a `+` above them to add a row or a column), a type badge (`abc` for text, `123` for numbers, `date` for dates, `dttm` for date-times, `time` for times, `T/F` for logicals) next to each column name, a summary of each column (see [Column summaries](#column-summaries)) and a filter box under each column name;
* the **status bar** with *Find in data*, how many rows and columns are on screen, the *Pages* button (see [Pages](#pages)), a summary of the selected cells and a summary of your changes.

The data editor will open in an RStudio `"dialog"` box by default, but can be optionally displayed in the RStudio viewer pane or a web browser by setting `viewer` to `"pane"` or `"browser"` respectively. The size of the dialog box is controlled by `viewer_width` and `viewer_height`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          viewer = "browser")
```

Row names (such as the car names in `mtcars`) are moved inside the table to a frozen `row names` column so that they can be edited, and the row indices are always displayed on the left-hand side to aid navigation. Only the visible rows are drawn in the browser, so scrolling through 100,000 rows is as smooth as scrolling through 10.

Once you are finished, close the data editor by hitting the `Done` button in the top right corner and the edited data will be returned. If you wish to discard all changes made to the data, select the `Cancel` button in the top left corner and the unedited data will be returned instead (or the value supplied to the `cancel` argument).

### 1.1 Column summaries

Under each column name is a small summary of the column, worked out from all of its rows (not only those on screen):

* a **histogram** for numbers and dates (dates are counted by year, month, day or hour, depending on how far apart they are);
* the **most common values** for text, `TRUE`/`FALSE` columns and columns with a few distinct values, as a bar split by how often each value appears;
* the **share of missing values** (in red) and the **number of distinct values**.

Hover over a bar to see what it counts. Click a bar to show only those rows, click the share of missing values to show the rows where the value is missing, or click the number of distinct values for the details: the smallest, largest, mean and median values and the standard deviation of numbers, or the earliest and latest dates.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("summaries.png")
```

The summaries are updated as you edit. Hide them with the `Summaries` button in the toolbar (the editor remembers your choice), or set `col_summary = FALSE` to leave them out.

### 1.2 Pages

Large data can be shown a page at a time. Click *Pages* in the status bar and choose how many rows and how many columns to show at once; the status bar then shows which rows and columns are on screen, with buttons to move to the previous, next, first and last page. Set `page_rows` and `page_cols` to open the editor in pages:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          page_rows = 10,
          page_cols = 6)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("pages.png")
```

Pages only change what is on screen. Filters count the rows of every page, *Find in data* goes to the page of each match, a paste wider than the page fills the columns of the next page, a new row is shown on the last page, and *Done*, *Export* and "Only what's on screen" cover every page.

## 2. Data Import

`data_edit()` can read in any form of tabular data from file for viewing and editing. By default `data_edit()` will use `read.csv` from the `utils` package to read in files, but this can be changed to any reading function by supplying the name of the function to the `read_fun` argument. If you need to pass any additional arguments to your reading function, these can be supplied as a named list to the `read_args` argument.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mtcars <- data_edit("mtcars.csv",
                    read_fun = "read.csv",
                    read_args = list(header = TRUE,
                                     row.names = 1))
head(mtcars)
```

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
head(mtcars)
```

The name of an object in your R session can also be supplied as a character string, e.g. `data_edit("mtcars")`.

### 2.1 Open other data without leaving the editor

The `Open` menu in the toolbar switches to other data without having to close the data editor. You can load any data frame, matrix or `dbplyr` table from your R session by name, upload a file (read with `read_fun` and `read_args`) or create a new empty table with a chosen number of rows and columns. Opening other data replaces the data in the editor, and `Done` returns the data that is open at the time.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("open-data.gif")
```

### 2.2 SPSS, Stata and SAS files

`data_edit()` reads SPSS (`.sav`, `.por`), Stata (`.dta`) and SAS (`.sas7bdat`, `.xpt`) files with the **haven** package, from a file name or from the `Open` menu, and edits data that was read with `haven` (or labelled with the **labelled** or **sjlabelled** packages) without losing its labels:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Read and edit an SPSS file, and save it again with its labels
data_edit("survey.sav", save_as = "survey.sav")

# Or edit data read with haven
survey <- haven::read_sav("survey.sav", user_na = TRUE)
survey <- data_edit(survey)
```

* **Variable labels** (what a column holds) are shown when you hover over a column name, in the column summary and in the `Form` tab.
* **Value labels** are shown next to the values (`1 Male`), and columns with value labels have an `lbl` badge. The cell editor lists the labels, and you can type or paste a label (`Female`) instead of its value (`2`). Other values can still be typed.
* **User-defined missing values** of SPSS files (e.g. `-99 No answer`) are shown in grey italics, count as missing in the column summaries and are kept as values.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("labelled.png")
```

Choose `Labels...` from a column's menu to change its variable label or its value labels, written one per line as `value = label`. The dialog shows how many rows have each value, and the change is recorded as one step in the code:

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("labels-dialog.png")
```

```r
survey <- survey %>%
  mutate(sex = structure(sex, labels = c("Male" = 1, "Female" = 2, "Refused" = 9, "Other" = 3)))
```

`Change type` turns a labelled column into a factor or text using its labels (`haven::as_factor()`), or into plain numbers (`haven::zap_labels()`). The returned data keeps the variable labels, value labels and missing values, and so does the generated code. When `save_as` ends in `.sav`, `.dta` or `.xpt` the data is written with `haven`, and the `Export` menu can download the data as an SPSS or Stata file.

### 2.3 Spatial data and list columns

Columns that hold a list per row, such as the geometry of an `sf` object, are shown as text (e.g. `MULTIPOLYGON (((-81.47 36.23, ...`) and cannot be edited, while the other columns can. `sf` objects are returned as `sf` objects with their geometry, so the attributes of spatial data can be edited in place:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(sf)
nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"))
nc <- data_edit(nc)
```

Data without any rows opens with one empty row to type in. The row is only returned once something has been entered in it.

## 3. Data Manipulation

`data_edit()` provides a variety of spreadsheet-style tools to edit your data. We will explore the use of each of these tools below, using `mtcars` as an example:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars)
```

Many of the tools can also be reached through the keyboard; press `?` inside the data editor or click the `?` button in the toolbar to see the full list of shortcuts (see [Keyboard shortcuts](#keyboard-shortcuts)).

### 3.1 Edit cells

Double-click a cell to edit it, then press `Enter` to save the new value or `Esc` to cancel. Values are checked against the type of the column: numbers are stored as numbers, dates as dates and `TRUE`/`FALSE` as logicals. Typing `NA` or clearing a cell stores a missing value.

Values typed in other common formats are converted for you: `1,234.5` or `45%` in a number column, `15/03/2024` in a date column (see [Copy and paste with spreadsheets](#copy-and-paste-with-spreadsheets) for how the order of day and month is decided) and `yes` or `no` in a `TRUE`/`FALSE` column.

If you type something that does not fit a number, date or `TRUE`/`FALSE` column, `data_edit()` asks what you would like to do instead of silently converting the whole column to text. You can store a missing value, convert the column to text or cancel the edit.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("edit-cells.gif")
```

### 3.2 Select, copy, paste, clear and fill

Click and drag (or `Shift` + click) to select a range of cells. The status bar shows the sum, mean and count of the selected numbers, just like a spreadsheet. Selected cells can be copied (`Ctrl+C`) and pasted (`Ctrl+V`) within the data editor or to and from other software such as Excel, cleared with `Delete`, or filled down with the value in the first row of the selection (`Ctrl+D`). A paste, fill or clear is a single step that can be undone. Click a column header to select the whole column.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("ranges.gif")
```

To fill cells like in a spreadsheet, drag the small square at the bottom-right corner of the selection down, up or across. The cells it passes over are outlined and filled when you let go:

* One selected value is copied into every cell.
* Two or more numbers, dates or texts ending in a number that go up (or down) by the same step carry on as a series: `1, 2` gives `3, 4, 5`, a week of dates gives the following weeks, month ends give the following month ends and `Week 1, Week 2` gives `Week 3, Week 4`.
* Anything else is repeated, e.g. `TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE`.
* Hold `Ctrl` when you let go to copy the selection without carrying on a series.

Like a paste, a fill is one step that can be undone and values that do not fit a column are asked about first. `Ctrl+D` (or `Fill down` in the right-click menu) copies the first row of the selection into the rows below it.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("fill.gif")
```

### 3.3 Copy and paste with spreadsheets

Copy cells in Excel, Google Sheets, LibreOffice or any other software that copies tables as text, click a cell in the data editor and press `Ctrl+V`:

* The block is pasted from the selected cell. Selecting a larger range that is a multiple of the block (e.g. ten cells for a single value) fills the range by repeating the block.
* If the block has more rows than there are below the selected cell, rows are added at the end of the data (unless `row_edit = FALSE`). If it has more columns than there are to the right, columns named `V1`, `V2`, ... are added at the end (unless `col_edit = FALSE`), in the same step.
* Press `Ctrl+Shift+V` instead to use the first row of the block as column names: the columns the block lands in are renamed (unless their names cannot be edited) and the columns it adds are named after it.
* Line endings from Windows, Mac or Linux, the line break that spreadsheets add after the last row, and cells containing line breaks, tabs or quotes are all handled.
* Values are converted to the type of their column. Formatted numbers such as `1,234.5`, `$12.50` or `45%` become `1234.5`, `12.5` and `0.45`. Dates such as `15/03/2024`, `15.03.2024` or `2024/3/15` become `2024-03-15`: whether the day or the month comes first is worked out from values such as `15/03` that can only be read one way, and otherwise follows the language of your browser (month first for US English). `yes`/`no`, `TRUE`/`FALSE` and `1`/`0` become logicals.
* If some values still do not fit their column (for example `n/a` in a numeric column, or a value that is not one of the options of a dropdown menu), the data editor asks once for the whole paste whether to store them as missing values, convert the column to text or cancel the paste.
* Read-only columns are skipped. When rows are filtered or columns are hidden, the block is pasted into the rows and columns on screen.
* A paste is a single step that can be undone, and the pasted cells are selected afterwards.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("paste.gif")
```

`Ctrl+C` copies the selected cells both as text and as a table, so they can be pasted into spreadsheets, documents or back into the data editor. Missing values are copied as empty cells, logicals as `TRUE` and `FALSE`, and cells containing line breaks or tabs are quoted, as spreadsheets expect.

### 3.4 Undo and redo

Every change can be undone with `Ctrl+Z` (or the undo button in the toolbar) and redone with `Ctrl+Y` (or the redo button). This includes edits, pasted ranges, cleared or filled cells, added or removed rows and columns, renamed columns and changes reverted from the review panel. A paste, fill or clear of many cells is undone in a single step, as shown at the end of the animation above. Undo and redo are also available from the right-click menus.

### 3.5 Addition or removal of rows or columns

Rows or columns can be added to the data from within the data editor by right clicking on a cell or a column header. Right-clicking a cell offers to insert rows above or below, delete the selected rows, fill down and insert a column to the left or right of the cell; right-clicking a column header offers to rename, insert, hide or delete columns.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("rows-columns.gif")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("column-menu.png")
```

New rows and columns can also be added at the end of the data from the `+` in the corner above the row numbers: choose `Add row` or `Add column`. New columns start empty and their type is worked out from the values you enter when the data is returned.

To move cells rather than whole rows, select the cells and choose `Insert cells, shift down` from the right-click menu: empty cells are inserted and the cells below them, in the selected columns only, move down (a row is added at the end when values would otherwise fall off). `Delete cells, shift up` removes the selected cells and moves the cells below them up. Both are one step that can be undone; clear the filters first, so that cells are not moved past rows that are hidden.

To prevent users from adding or removing rows or columns, set `row_edit = FALSE` or `col_edit = FALSE` respectively.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          row_edit = FALSE,
          col_edit = FALSE)
```

### 3.6 Rename rows or columns

`data_edit()` has full support for editing row and column names. Double-click the name of a column (or choose `Rename column` from its menu) to rename it; the new name must be unique and cannot be empty. Row names are edited like any other cell in the `row names` column, and must be unique: a name that another row already has is refused and the cell goes back to its old name. The row indices cannot be edited. To keep the row names out of sight (they are still returned), set `row_names = FALSE`.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("rename-resize.gif")
```

To prevent users from editing column names, set `col_names = FALSE` or supply the names of the columns that cannot be renamed. For example, if we only wanted to prevent users from renaming the `mpg` column:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          col_names = "mpg")
```

### 3.7 Resize columns

To resize columns, go to the right-hand border of the header of that column and drag the cursor to the desired width (shown at the end of the animation above). Columns keep their width while you edit, including when changes are undone or redone. Columns start as wide as their values, but no wider than 320 pixels, so long text does not push the other columns off screen. Set the starting widths in pixels with `col_widths`, either one width for every column or widths by column name:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(samples,
          col_widths = c(notes = 400, id = 60))
```

To make the columns fill the width of the editor instead, see [Stretch columns to fill page](#stretch-columns-to-fill-page).

### 3.8 Find values

Press `Ctrl+F` or click `Find in data` in the status bar to search the rows and columns on screen. The first matching cell is selected and the number of matches is shown (e.g. `1 of 7`); press `Enter` to jump to the next match, `Shift+Enter` to go back and `Esc` to clear the search.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("find.gif")
```

### 3.9 Append columns or rows

`data_edit()` can perform `rbind` and `cbind` operations internally to append new rows or columns to the data prior to editing. The new rows or columns can be supplied as a matrix or data.frame, a named list or, for empty rows or columns, a vector of names to the `row_bind` or `col_bind` arguments. If binding both rows and columns, it is important to note that rows are bound before columns.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# New column to add
new_col <- matrix(rep(NA, nrow(mtcars)),
                  ncol = 1,
                  dimnames = list(NULL, "test"))

# Edit data with new column added
data_edit(mtcars,
          col_bind = new_col)

# Add two empty rows and an empty column called "notes"
data_edit(mtcars,
          row_bind = c("New car 1", "New car 2"),
          col_bind = "notes")
```

### 3.10 Read-only and hidden columns

If you would like to prevent values from being edited in certain columns, you can supply the names of the columns that cannot be edited to the `col_readonly` argument. Read-only columns show a lock next to their name, and their values and names cannot be changed. For example, if we wanted to prevent the `mpg` column from being edited:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          col_readonly = "mpg")
```

Columns that users should not see at all can be supplied to `col_hide`. Hidden columns cannot be viewed or edited, but they are kept in place in the returned data.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          col_hide = c("vs", "am"))
```

### 3.11 Factor columns

`data_edit()` fully supports data frames with factor columns, including ordered factors. Factor columns are edited as text, so you can freely enter new values without encountering errors, and are returned as factors with their original levels in their original order. New values become new levels after the existing ones, and levels that are no longer used are kept, as R does when values of a factor are replaced.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Create data with a factor column
df <- data.frame(
  name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie"),
  group = factor(c("A", "B", "A"))
)

# Change Bob's group to "C" in the editor
df_edited <- data_edit(df)
levels(df_edited$group)
#> [1] "A" "B" "C"
```

Character columns are returned as text. Set `col_factor = TRUE` to turn them into factors as well (their levels are sorted, as `factor()` does).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
df_edited <- data_edit(df, col_factor = TRUE)
class(df_edited$name)
#> [1] "factor"
```

### 3.12 Change whole columns

Click the `⋮` button in a column's header (or right-click the header) for actions that change the whole column at once. Each action opens a dialog that previews the result before you apply it:

* **Formula...**: add a new column, or replace the values of the column, with an R expression worked out for every row, e.g. `round(mpg * 0.425, 1)`, `paste(first, last)` or `case_when(ph < 7 ~ "acidic", ph > 7 ~ "basic", .default = "neutral")`. Formulas can use column names, numbers, text in quotes and common functions (arithmetic, `round()`, `ifelse()`, `paste()`, `substr()`, `as.Date()`, `case_when()`, `if_else()`, `lag()`, `row_number()`, ...), but not other R code, so they are safe to offer in shiny apps.
* **Find and replace...**: replace text within cells (matching case or not, or with a regular expression), or replace whole cells. For numbers and dates whole cells are replaced; leave `Find` empty to fill missing values, or `Replace with` empty to clear the cells.
* **Recode values...**: lists the values of the column, the most common first, with a box to type a new value for each.
* **Change type**: number, whole number, text, `TRUE`/`FALSE`, date or factor. If some values cannot be converted (e.g. `"x"` to a date), you are told which ones before they become missing.
* **Sort ascending** / **Sort descending**: put the rows in order of the column.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("column-actions.png")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("formula.png")
```

Each action is recorded as a single `dplyr` verb, so the code that reproduces your edits (see [Exporting Code](#exporting-code)) says what you did, rather than listing every value that changed:

```r
samples <- samples %>%
  mutate(ph_class = case_when(ph < 7 ~ "acidic", ph > 7 ~ "basic", .default = "neutral"), .after = ph) %>%
  mutate(site = case_match(site, "North" ~ "north", .default = site))
```

The editor applies an action by running that same verb on your data, so the code always gives exactly the result you saw. Actions can be undone like any other change, and appear in the `History` tab with their code. Set `col_actions = FALSE` to remove them from the column menu.

### 3.13 Edit one record at a time

Wide tables are easier to fill in one record (row) at a time. Click `Form` in the toolbar, or the `Form` tab of the side panel, to see the selected row as a form with a labelled field for each visible column:

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("record.png")
```

* The fields use the same inputs as the grid (dropdown menus, dates, `TRUE`/`FALSE`, ...) and the same checks, so a value that does not fit its column asks whether to store `NA`.
* Press `Enter` to save a field and move to the next one.
* Broken [validation rules](#validation-rules) are shown under the fields they concern, and changed fields are marked.
* The arrows move to the previous or next row on screen (filters apply), and the grid follows; selecting a cell in the grid shows its row in the form.
* `New` adds a row at the end and puts the cursor in its first field.

Changes made in the form are ordinary edits: they can be undone, are listed in the review panel and appear in the code.

### 3.14 Comments on cells

Right-click a cell and choose `Add comment` (or select it and press `Shift+F2`) to leave a comment on it: why a value was changed, what still needs checking or where it came from. Press `Ctrl+Enter` or `Save` to keep the comment and `Escape` to close it without saving. Commented cells have an amber corner; rest the pointer on the cell (or open the record form) to read the comment, and right-click it to edit or delete it. To start afresh, right-click any cell and choose `Delete all comments`; the editor asks first, as deleted comments cannot be brought back with undo.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("comments.png")
```

Comments are returned with the data as the `comments` attribute, a data frame with the `row` (its number in the returned data), the `column`, the `comment`, the `user` who wrote it and the `time`. Data that has this attribute opens with its comments, so they can be kept from one session to the next. Rows can also be given by their row names:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
cars <- data_edit(mtcars)
attr(cars, "comments")
#>   row column                       comment user                time
#> 1   3    mpg Checked against the 1974 table  ana 2026-11-02 09:27:27

# Comments of your own
attr(mtcars, "comments") <- data.frame(row = "Datsun 710", column = "mpg",
                                       comment = "Checked against the 1974 table")
data_edit(mtcars)
```

Comments are kept in [drafts](#unsaved-changes-are-kept) with the changes, but they are not changes to the data: they are not undone and not listed in the review panel.

## 4. Data Creation

You can also use `data_edit()` to interactively create data.frames from scratch without any coding.

### 4.1 Start with empty template

If no data is supplied to `data_edit()` an empty data.frame will be constructed with 10 rows and columns. You can then build your data.frame from scratch by adding new rows and columns and annotating the cells.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit()
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("template-empty.png")
```

The dimensions of the template can be controlled by supplying a vector of the form `c(nrow, ncol)` to indicate the number of rows and columns to use.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(c(20, 15))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("template-size.png")
```

### 4.2 Start with a labelled template

Alternatively, you can pass a vector of column names to create a data.frame template with pre-defined column names. Use the `+` above the row numbers (`Add row`) to add as many rows as you need.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(c("Date", "Country", "Temperature", "Rainfall", "Visibility", "Humidity"))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("template.gif")
```

The columns of a template are typed automatically when the data is returned, so a column in which you only entered numbers is returned as a numeric column.

## 5. Data Filtering

`data_edit()` makes it easy to view and edit a subset of your data: filter rows by typing under the column headers or in the `Filters` panel, and show or hide columns from the `Select` menu. Edits made to a subset are applied directly to the complete dataset.

### 5.1 Row filtering

Every column has a filter box under its name and the box depends on the type of the column:

* **numbers** have `min` and `max` boxes to keep values within a range;
* **columns with a few distinct values** (e.g. `cyl` or `gear`) have a list to pick one or more values (`Any` means no filter);
* **text** columns keep values that contain what you type; start with `!` (e.g. `!set`) to keep the values that do not contain it.

Clicking a bar of a column's summary (see [Column summaries](#column-summaries)) sets its filter for you, and clicking the share of missing values shows only the rows where the value is missing. Rows must match every filter to be shown. Active filters are listed as chips in the toolbar; click the `x` on a chip to remove that filter or `Clear filters` to remove them all. With more than four filters the toolbar shows the first three and a `+2 more` button that opens the `Filters` panel. The status bar shows how many of the rows are on screen.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("filter-rows.gif")
```

### 5.2 Filters panel

Click `Filters` in the toolbar to see and change every filter in one place, which is the easiest way to build a complex combination of filters. The panel opens beside the grid, and the grid follows it as you work: there is nothing to apply.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("filter-panel.png")
```

Click `Add filter` and pick a column: type to find it, and use the arrow keys and `Enter` or click it. Each filter is a card that asks for what suits its column:

* **Numbers, dates and date-times** show a histogram of the column with a range on it. Drag the ends of the range (or use the arrow keys, `Page Up`, `Page Down`, `Home` and `End`), or type them in the boxes below it. The bars of the rows that are kept are highlighted.
* **Columns with a few values** (text, factors, dropdowns) list their values with how many rows have each, missing values too. Tick the values to keep; long lists can be searched.
* **Logical columns** have `TRUE`, `FALSE` and `missing` buttons with their counts.
* **Text** is searched for words: type one and press `Enter`, or pick one of the values of the column listed under the box with how many rows have each (the most common when there are many). Rows that contain any of the words are kept. A pattern can start from one of those values too.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "40%"}
screenshot("filter-values.png")
```

The menu at the top of a card changes the condition, and a column can have more than one card:

| Condition                                              | Keeps the rows where the value                    | Columns               |
|--------------------------------------------------------|---------------------------------------------------|-----------------------|
| `is any of`, `is none of`                              | is (or is not) one of the values                  | all                   |
| `is above`, `is below`, `is at least`, `is at most`    | compares that way with the value                  | numbers, dates, times |
| `is between`, `is not between`                         | lies (or does not lie) between two values         | numbers, dates, times |
| `contains`, `does not contain`                         | includes (or does not include) any of the words   | all except logicals   |
| `matches the pattern`, `does not match the pattern`    | matches (or does not match) a regular expression  | all except logicals   |
| `is missing`, `is not missing`                         | is (or is not) missing                            | all                   |

* `is between` includes both ends, like `dplyr::between()` and the boxes under the column headers, and the ends can be given in either order. Use `is above` and `is below` to leave them out.
* `contains` looks for plain text and ignores case, so `merc` finds `Merc 230`. It searches what the cells show: the names of dropdown choices and the text of HTML columns without their tags. `matches the pattern` takes a regular expression and respects case, so `^Merc [0-9]+$` finds `Merc 230` and not `Merc 450SE`. The patterns are JavaScript regular expressions, so classes such as `[[:alpha:]]` are written `[a-zA-Z]`.
* `is none of`, `is not between`, `does not contain` and `does not match the pattern` also keep the rows where the value is missing.
* The values of password columns are never listed; type them instead.

Each card says how many rows it keeps on its own, and the bottom of the panel how many rows are shown. A card that is `not set yet`, or has a mistake (text where a number is needed, a pattern that is not a regular expression), is left out until it is finished. Click the name of a column to fold or open its card, the `x` to remove it, and `Clear all` to remove every filter.

With two filters or more, choose whether rows must match **all** of them (the default) or **any** of them. In the toolbar, filters that match any are listed after `Any of:`.

Filters set under the column headers or from a column's summary are listed in the panel too (`!text` in a header box as `does not contain`), with where they come from. They stay where they are while you leave them unchanged; if you change one, it becomes a filter of the panel and its box under the header is cleared. Choosing `any` makes them filters of the panel as well, so that they are part of the "or".

### 5.3 Column selection

Click `Select` in the toolbar to show or hide columns, or choose `Hide column` from the menu of a column header. `Show all` and `Hide all` change every column at once, and the button shows how many columns are visible.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("select-columns.gif")
```

Columns can also be hidden before the data editor opens (`col_hide`, see [Read-only and hidden columns](#read-only-and-hidden-columns)); those columns are not listed in the `Select` menu and cannot be shown by the user.

### 5.4 Edits apply to the complete dataset

Filtered rows and hidden columns are only *views* onto your data, so any change you make while a filter is active is made directly to the complete dataset, without requiring any additional action (earlier versions of **DataEditR** needed a *sync* button for this). Rows added while a filter is active stay visible until the filters change, so you can fill them in even if they do not match the filters yet.

### 5.5 Return or export data subsets

`data_edit()` will return the complete dataset as an R object for downstream use by default. If you would like to return just the rows and columns that are on screen, open the menu next to the `Done` button and choose `Only what's on screen` before pressing `Done`. The menu shows the size of the data that each option returns.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("done-export.gif")
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mtcars_subset <- data_edit(mtcars)
str(mtcars_subset)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
mtcars_subset <- mtcars[mtcars$cyl %in% c(4, 6) & mtcars$mpg >= 20,
                        c("mpg", "cyl", "disp", "hp", "wt", "gear", "carb")]
str(mtcars_subset)
```

## 6. Data Saving

`data_edit()` will automatically return the edited data with appropriate column classes as an R object for use within R. Matrices, tibbles and data.tables are returned with their original class, and the type of each column is kept: numbers stay numbers, dates stay dates and text that looks like a number (e.g. `"001"`) stays text. Factor columns are returned as factors with their levels, while character columns are not converted to factors unless `col_factor = TRUE` is set (see [Factor columns](#factor-columns)).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Add character column
mtcars_new <- cbind(rownames(mtcars), mtcars)
colnames(mtcars_new)[1] <- "car"

# Convert characters to factors
mtcars_new <- data_edit(mtcars_new,
                        col_factor = TRUE)
str(mtcars_new)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE}
mtcars_new <- cbind(rownames(mtcars), mtcars)
colnames(mtcars_new)[1] <- "car"
mtcars_new$car <- factor(mtcars_new$car)
str(mtcars_new)
```

The edited data can also be written to a file of any format by specifying the name of the file to the `save_as` argument and specifying the name of the writing function to use through `write_fun`. The default is to use `write.csv` from the `utils` package. You can also pass any additional arguments to your write function in a named list to `write_args`. The data will be written to file when the `Done` button is selected, and a message says where it was saved; untick `Also save to` in the `Done` menu to close the editor without saving. Data that has no row names (only row numbers) is written without them unless `write_args` sets `row.names`. `read_fun` and `write_fun` can name functions of other packages, e.g. `read_fun = "readxl::read_excel"`, and `save_as` does not have to be a file: with `write_fun = "googlesheets4::write_sheet"` it can be a Google Sheet.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mtcars_new <- data_edit(mtcars,
                        save_as = "mtcars.csv",
                        write_fun = "write.table",
                        write_args = list(sep = ",",
                                          row.names = TRUE))
```

Alternatively, data can be downloaded to file at any time from the `Export` menu in the toolbar, either all data or only what is on screen. Files are named after `save_as` (with `-subset` added for subsets), or after today's date if `save_as` is not supplied, and are written with `write_fun` and `write_args`.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("export-menu.png")
```

## 7. Complex user inputs

`data_edit()` can also be used to accept complex inputs from users, and these inputs can be restricted, by giving columns a specific input such as checkboxes, dropdown menus, date pickers, numbers within limits or ratings. To use this feature, the inputs for the columns must be supplied in a named list through the `col_options` argument. Columns with options can still be renamed, and users can still add or remove other columns.

| `col_options` entry | Input | Returned as |
|---------------------|-------|-------------|
| `c(TRUE, FALSE)` or `"checkbox"` | checkbox | logical |
| `c("A", "B", "C")` | dropdown menu of the values | character (numeric for numbers in a numeric column) |
| `"dropdown"` | dropdown menu of the values in the column (the levels of a factor) | as the column |
| `"date"` | date picker | `Date` |
| `"datetime"` | date and time picker | `POSIXct` |
| `"time"` | time picker | character (`"HH:MM"`) |
| `"textarea"` | text over several lines | character |
| `"password"` | hidden text | character |
| `"url"` | web address with a button to open it | character |
| `"colour"` (or `"color"`) | colour with a swatch | character |
| `c(min = 0, max = 10, step = 0.5)` | number within limits (any of the three), in steps of `step` from `min` | numeric |
| `"integer"` or `list(type = "integer", min = 0, max = 10)` | whole number (within limits) | integer |
| `"slider"` or `c(type = "slider", min = 0, max = 1, step = 0.05)` | slider and bar for numbers within limits (0 to 100 by default) | numeric |
| `"rating"` or `c(type = "rating", stars = 10)` | star rating (5 stars by default) | numeric |

Columns are converted to the type their input needs when the data editor opens, and values that do not fit a column's input, whether typed or pasted, are caught before they are stored. Values already in the data that do not fit (for example a value above the maximum of a slider, or a value that is not one of the options of a dropdown menu) are kept but marked with a red line, and hovering over them says why.

Columns named in `col_options`, `col_readonly`, `col_hide` or `col_widths` that are not in the data are ignored, with a message, so the same settings can be used for different data (for example in a shiny app where the data changes).

The limits of sliders and numbers and the number of stars of ratings can be customised by giving the type together with its settings:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(samples,
          col_options = list(
            # proportions from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.05
            done = c(type = "slider", min = 0, max = 1, step = 0.05),
            # a rating out of 10 stars
            quality = c(type = "rating", stars = 10),
            # numbers from 0 to 14 (type = "number" is optional here)
            ph = c(min = 0, max = 14, step = 0.1)
          ))
```

`list(type = "slider", min = 0, max = 1, step = 0.05)` works too. A slider without settings runs from 0 to 100 in steps of 1, and a rating has 5 stars.

The animations in this section use the following data, with all four kinds of input and a read-only `mpg` column:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
cars <- data.frame(
  car = rownames(mtcars)[1:10],
  mpg = mtcars$mpg[1:10],
  fast = mtcars$mpg[1:10] > 21,
  colour = c("red", "blue", "black", "green", "red",
             "orange", "blue", "black", "green", "red"),
  bought = as.Date("2024-01-15") + c(0, 31, 45, 90, 120, 151, 200, 230, 260, 301),
  pin = c("4821", "1937", "5560", "0042", "7713",
          "2468", "1357", "9090", "3141", "2718")
)

data_edit(cars,
          col_options = list(fast = c(TRUE, FALSE),
                             colour = c("red", "blue", "orange", "green", "black"),
                             bought = "date",
                             pin = "password"),
          col_readonly = "mpg")
```

### 7.1 Checkboxes

Checkboxes can be used to obtain `TRUE` or `FALSE` value inputs from users. Double-click a checkbox cell and click the box (or press `Space`) to change its value; ticked cells are returned as `TRUE`. A new checkbox column can be added to existing data with `col_bind`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          col_bind = "fast",
          col_options = list(fast = c(TRUE, FALSE)))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("col-checkbox.gif")
```

### 7.2 Dropdown menus

Dropdown menus can be used to help prevent typing errors when a set number of options are available for a column. For example, if we have a factor with levels `Treatment-A`, `Treatment-B` or `Treatment-C` it would be easier to select these options from a dropdown menu instead of having to manually type them. Dropdown menus can be added in the same way as checkboxes.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Add column for car colour
data_edit(mtcars,
          col_bind = "colour",
          col_options = list(colour = c("red",
                                        "blue",
                                        "orange",
                                        "green",
                                        "black")))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("col-dropdown.gif")
```

Typing in a dropdown cell narrows the list down to the matching options, and only the listed options can be entered.

To show names that differ from the values that are stored, give the options as a named list (as for `shiny::selectInput()`). The cells, the menu and the filter show the names, the data keeps the values, and typing or pasting a name stores its value:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(sites,
          col_options = list(state = list(`New South Wales` = "NSW",
                                          Victoria = "VIC",
                                          Queensland = "QLD")))
```

To offer the values that are already in a column, give `"dropdown"` on its own. Factors offer their levels, other columns their distinct values:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(iris, col_options = list(Species = "dropdown"))
```

### 7.3 Dates

Dates can be entered interactively by selecting the relevant day from a calendar. To convert a column to accept interactive date inputs, supply a list with the name of the column and `"date"` as the option to `col_options`. The column is returned as a `Date` column.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(c("date", "time", "region", "temperature"),
          col_options = list(date = "date", time = "time"))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("col-date.gif")
```

### 7.4 Passwords

If you would like to keep your data entries a secret, you can convert relevant columns to accept passwords as inputs. The data is entered as per usual, but the values are displayed as dots to conceal the entered data. To convert a column to accept password inputs, supply a list with the name of the column and `"password"` as the option to `col_options`.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(c("date", "time", "user", "password"),
          col_options = list(password = "password"))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("col-password.gif")
```

The values are only hidden on screen: they are returned (and saved with `save_as`) as plain text.

### 7.5 More column types

The animation below uses sample records with the other column types:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
samples <- data.frame(
  sample = c("S-01", "S-02", "S-03", "S-04", "S-05"),
  notes = c("Clear.\nStored at 4\u00b0C", "Slightly cloudy", NA,
            "Re-run\nfollowing QC", "Clear"),
  received = c("2024-03-15 09:30:00", "2024-03-15 11:05:00",
               "2024-03-16 08:45:00", NA, "2024-03-18 14:20:00"),
  start = c("09:30", "10:15", NA, "13:00", "15:45"),
  ph = c(7.1, 6.8, 7.4, NA, 7.0),
  done = c(100, 60, 25, 0, 80),
  quality = c(5, 3, 4, NA, 2),
  protocol = c("https://www.protocols.io", NA, "https://www.r-project.org",
               NA, NA),
  label = c("#1D4ED8", "orange", "seagreen", "#E11D48", "purple")
)

data_edit(samples,
          col_options = list(notes = "textarea",
                             received = "datetime",
                             start = "time",
                             ph = c(min = 0, max = 14, step = 0.1),
                             done = "slider",
                             quality = "rating",
                             protocol = "url",
                             label = "colour"))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("col-types.png")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("col-types.gif")
```

* **Text over several lines** (`"textarea"`): the cell grows to show every line. `Enter` saves the text like in any other cell, while `Shift+Enter` or `Alt+Enter` starts a new line.
* **Date-times and times** (`"datetime"`, `"time"`): pickers for both. Date-time columns are returned as `POSIXct`; times are returned as text such as `"14:30"`, which `as.difftime()` or the `hms` package can convert. Columns that are already `POSIXct` can be typed into without an option (e.g. `2024-03-15 14:30`).
* **Numbers within limits** (`c(min = , max = , step = )`): values outside the limits are flagged, and the `step` sets how much the arrows of the number box change the value.
* **Sliders and ratings** (`"slider"`, `"rating"`): a bar shows each value; double-click to drag the slider (or use the arrow keys) or to click a star. Clear a cell with `Delete` to store a missing value.
* **Web addresses** (`"url"`): addresses starting with `http://`, `https://` or `mailto:` get a button that opens them in a new tab; double-click the cell to edit the address.
* **HTML** (`"html"`): the cells are shown as HTML, e.g. `Photo:<br/><a href="https://...">details</a>` as a line break and a link that opens in a new tab. Text formatting, lists, links and images are shown; scripts, styles, forms and event handlers are removed. Double-click a cell to edit its HTML.
* **Colours** (`"colour"`): a swatch is shown next to each colour, for R colour names such as `"grey50"` or `"steelblue"` and hex codes such as `"#1D4ED8"`; values that are not colours get a dashed swatch. Double-click a cell to type a colour or pick one: the swatches offer the colours already in the column, R's palette and the colour-blind-safe Okabe-Ito palette, and `Other colour...` opens the browser's colour picker. Set the swatches with e.g. `list(type = "colour", palette = c("steelblue", "darkorange", "#009E73"))`.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("colour-picker.png")
```

### 7.6 Validation rules

Column inputs stop values that do not fit a single cell. Rules check the data as a whole: that values are filled in, unique or within limits, or that columns agree with each other. Supply them to `rules` as one-sided formulas that are `TRUE` for valid rows, named with the message to show:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(samples,
          rules = list(
            "pH is between 0 and 14" = ~ ph >= 0 & ph <= 14,
            "The end is after the start" = ~ end >= start,
            "Every sample has an ID" = ~ !is.na(sample),
            "Sample IDs are unique" = ~ !duplicated(sample)
          ))
```

Rules are checked after every change. Cells that break a rule get a red corner and a tooltip with the message, the status bar counts the problems and the `Problems` tab lists them; click a row to go to it. Missing values pass a rule unless it says otherwise, so `end >= start` only checks rows where both dates are filled in.

You can also add rules from a column's menu (`Rules...`): make the column required or unique, set the smallest and largest values of numbers and dates, give a pattern that text must match (a regular expression such as `S-[0-9]{2}`) or write a formula. The dialog shows how many rows break the rules before you save them.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("rules-dialog.png")
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("problems.png")
```

When rules are broken, `Done` asks whether to return the data anyway or keep editing. In shiny apps, `dataEditProblems()` returns the problems, for example to disable a *Save* button until they are fixed.

### 7.7 Conditional formatting

Conditional formats colour cells by their values, to make the data easier to read. They change how cells look, not the data. Supply them to `formats`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          formats = list(
            # cells of mpg above 22 in green
            "Fast" = list(~ mpg > 22, fill = "#DCFCE7", color = "#166534"),
            # whole rows of V8 cars in yellow
            "V8" = list(~ cyl == 8, fill = "lightyellow", columns = "all"),
            # hp shaded from white (lowest) to red (highest)
            list(scale = c("white", "#F87171"), columns = "hp")
          ))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("formats.png")
```

A rule is a one-sided formula that is `TRUE` for the rows to colour, with a `fill`, a text `color` and/or `bold = TRUE` (a formula on its own gets a yellow fill). It colours the cells of the columns the formula uses; give `columns` to colour other columns, or `columns = "all"` to colour whole rows. A colour scale shades the numbers of its `columns` from the first colour (the lowest value) to the last (the highest); give three colours for a middle colour, `limits = c(0, 300)` to fix the values of the end colours and `mid` for the value of the middle one. Colours can be R colour names or hex codes. When several formats colour a cell, the later one wins.

Formats are updated after every change. You can also add them from a column's menu (`Conditional formatting...`): highlight the cells of the column, or whole rows, where the value is greater or less than a value, between two values, equal to a value, contains some text, is blank, duplicated, above or below average, among the highest or lowest, or makes a formula `TRUE`; or shade the column with a colour scale. The dialog shows how many rows match before the format is added, and lists the column's formats with the code to add each one to `formats`, so that it can be kept in your script.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("formats-dialog.png")
```

## 8. Customisation

`data_edit()` has been designed to be simple, but does come with some customisation options including column stretching, addition of logos and/or titles, custom themes and the option to hide the menus.

### 8.1 Stretch columns to fill page

If you would like to make full use of the space available to you, you can set `col_stretch = TRUE` to stretch the columns to fill the full width of the display.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(iris,
          col_stretch = TRUE)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("stretch.png")
```

### 8.2 Logo and title

`data_edit()` does also have support for adding a logo and/or title to the data editor. For example, if you wanted to use `data_edit()` within your own package you can customise it with your package `logo` (the path or URL of an image) and instructions to the user through `title`. Use `logo_size` to set the width of the logo in pixels and `logo_side` to place it on the `"left"` or `"right"` of the title.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
logo <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/DillonHammill/DataEditR/master/man/figures/logo.png"
data_edit(mtcars,
          logo = logo,
          logo_size = 26,
          title = "Car data")
```

### 8.3 Custom themes

`data_edit()` uses Bootstrap 5 through the `bslib` package. You can explore the different themes by supplying the name of a [Bootswatch](https://bootswatch.com/) theme to the `theme` argument. Alternatively, you can create your own custom `bs_theme` and supply that object to `theme` instead.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# Preset theme
data_edit(
  mtcars,
  theme = "flatly"
)

# Custom theme
library(bslib)
custom_theme <- bs_theme(
  version = 5,
  primary = "#7C3AED",
  base_font = font_google("Lato")
)
data_edit(
  mtcars,
  theme = custom_theme
)
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("custom.png")
```

### 8.4 Simplified editor

Set `hide = TRUE` to hide the `Open` and `Export` menus and the options of the `Done` button, for example when `data_edit()` is used to collect data from users. When `save_as` is supplied the data is still written to file when `Done` is pressed.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(c("Name", "Email", "Attending"),
          col_options = list(Attending = c(TRUE, FALSE)),
          save_as = "rsvp.csv",
          hide = TRUE)
```

## 9. Reviewing and tracking changes

`data_edit()` keeps track of every change you make, so you can see what has changed before you hit `Done` and revert any change on its own.

### 9.1 Review changes

The status bar summarises your changes (e.g. `2 cells edited · 1 row added`) and the `Review` button shows how many changes there are. Click it to open the review panel, which lists every edited, added, removed or renamed cell, row and column with its old and new value. Click the name of a row to jump to it in the grid, `Revert` (or `Remove` / `Restore`) to undo that one change, or `Revert all` to go back to the original data. Reverts can be undone with `Ctrl+Z` like any other change.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("review.gif")
```

### 9.2 Highlight changed cells

Cells that have been edited or added compared to the original data are highlighted with a blue tint and border. Any cell whose value differs from the original, as well as all cells in newly added rows or columns, is highlighted. Highlights follow undo, redo and reverts, and inserting rows or columns does not cause other cells to appear changed.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("track.png")
```

You can pass any valid CSS color to `track` to customise the highlight colour, or `track = FALSE` to turn the highlighting off. For example, to use red:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          track = "red")
```

### 9.3 History and notes

The `History` tab of the review panel lists every change in the order it was made, newest first: what was changed, by whom (hover over the time) and how, so a paste, a fill, a cleared range, an undo or a revert each show as one step. Undoing a change does not remove it from the history; it is added as a new step, so the history is a complete record of the session.

Click `Add note` under a step to say why the change was made, for example where a corrected value came from. Press `Enter` to save the note or `Escape` to leave it as it was.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("history.png")
```

### 9.4 Keep a change log

Supply the name of a csv file to `log` to keep the history when you press `Done`. Each change becomes one row with the `data` that was edited, the `time`, the `user`, the `step` and `how` it was made (and the `code` of column actions), the `action` (`edit`, `add row`, `remove row`, `add column`, `remove column` or `rename column`), the `row` (its row name, or its number in the data you opened), the `column`, the `old` and `new` values and the `note`. New changes are added to the end of the file, so one file can keep the history of every editing session of a dataset or a project:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
lab <- data_edit("lab_results.csv",
                 save_as = "lab_results.csv",
                 log = "lab_results_log.csv")

log <- read.csv("lab_results_log.csv")
log[, c("time", "user", "how", "row", "column", "old", "new", "note")]
#>                       time user   how row column old  new                            note
#> 1 2026-11-01 14:02:11+1100  ana  edit   3     pH 7.9  7.4 Re-measured, meter recalibrated
#> 2 2026-11-01 14:03:40+1100  ana paste  12   mass 1.2 1.25                            <NA>
```

Each editing session gets its own `session` value (when it started), and the `History` tab lists the earlier sessions of the same data kept in the file below the changes of this session, newest first. Click a session to see its steps and notes:

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("history-sessions.png")
```

`log` can also be a function, which is called with the log as a data frame, for example to write it to a database. Nothing is written when `Cancel` is pressed. The user name is the name you are logged in with; set `options(DataEditR.user = "Your Name")` to record another name.

### 9.5 Unsaved changes are kept

While you edit, `data_edit()` saves your changes as a draft a moment after each change. If the editor is closed without pressing `Done` or `Cancel` (the window was closed by accident, R crashed or the computer restarted), open the same data again and you are offered your unsaved changes:

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("restore.png")
```

`Restore changes` brings back the data as you left it, with its history and notes, and each restored step can still be undone. `Discard changes` throws the draft away. Pressing `Cancel` asks before your changes are thrown away.

Drafts are kept in `tools::R_user_dir("DataEditR", "data")` and are removed when you press `Done` or `Cancel`, when they are restored or discarded, and after 30 days. Use `options(DataEditR.drafts = "path/to/folder")` to keep them elsewhere, or `autosave = FALSE` to turn drafts off.

### 9.6 Change tracking in shiny modules

Change tracking is also available when the data editor is used in your own shiny applications through `dataEditServer()`. `dataEditChanges()` returns a summary of the changes that have not been saved yet, `dataEditLog()` returns the change log and `dataEditCommit()` saves the changes (and returns the log of what it saved), after which the highlights are cleared. Set `autosave = TRUE` in `dataEditServer()` to keep drafts for each user of the app:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(shiny)
library(DataEditR)

ui <- fluidPage(
  actionButton("save", "Save"),
  textOutput("unsaved"),
  dataEditUI("edit")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  edited <- dataEditServer("edit",
                           data = reactive(mtcars),
                           track = TRUE)
  output$unsaved <- renderText({
    paste(dataEditChanges(edited)$total, "unsaved changes")
  })
  observeEvent(input$save, {
    dataEditCommit(edited)
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

## 10. Keyboard shortcuts

| Action                  | Shortcut                      |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------|
| Edit cell               | Double-click                  |
| Save / cancel edit      | `Enter` / `Esc`               |
| New line in a text area | `Shift+Enter` or `Alt+Enter`  |
| Undo / redo             | `Ctrl+Z` / `Ctrl+Y`           |
| Select a range          | Click and drag, `Shift`+click |
| Copy / paste range (also to and from spreadsheets) | `Ctrl+C` / `Ctrl+V` |
| Clear selected cells    | `Delete`                      |
| Fill down               | `Ctrl+D`                      |
| Find in data            | `Ctrl+F`, then `Enter` / `Shift+Enter` |
| Rename column           | Double-click column name      |
| Row and column menus    | Right-click                   |
| Show the shortcuts      | `?`                           |

Use `Cmd` instead of `Ctrl` on a Mac.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("shortcuts.png")
```

## 11. RStudio Add-in

`DataEditR` also ships with an RStudio add-in should you prefer to interact with your data in this way. Simply highlight the name of a dataset in an active script or the console and select `Interactive Data Editor` from the list of `Addins` in your RStudio session. If nothing is highlighted, an empty table is opened instead. The add-in can be bound to a keyboard shortcut through `Tools > Modify Keyboard Shortcuts...`.

## 12. Databases

`data_edit()` can also edit tables stored in a database. Connect with `DBI`, pass a `dbplyr` lazy table (optionally filtered) to `data_edit()` and the rows are loaded into the editor. Changes are staged while you edit and written to the database in a single transaction when you press `Done` and confirm the summary of changes.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(dplyr)
con <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), "cars.sqlite")

data_edit(tbl(con, "cars") %>% filter(cyl == 6))
```

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("db-commit.gif")
```

The same editor can be added to your own shiny apps, where `dataEditCommit()` writes the changes to the database (for example when a *Save* button is pressed) and `dataEditChanges()` summarises what will be written. See `vignette("databases", package = "DataEditR")` for how to connect to different databases, how rows are matched to the database, saving changes from shiny apps and what happens when someone else changes the data while you are editing it.

## 13. Interactively Edit Googlesheets

`DataEditR` can also be used to interactively edit googlesheets using `googlesheets4`. Simply authorise `googlesheets4`, create a new sheet, edit the data using `data_edit()` and write the edited data to the created sheet.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(googlesheets4)

# Authorise
gs4_auth(
  email = "username@gmail.com"
)

# Create a sheet
ss <- gs4_create(
  "mtcars"
)

# Edit data
mtcars_new <- data_edit(
  mtcars,
  save_as = ss,
  write_fun = "write_sheet",
  write_args = list(sheet = "mtcars")
)
```

## 14. Exporting Code

For reproducibility, it is possible to export the code required to generate the final edited version of your data. The generated code uses tidyverse-style `dplyr` verbs to transform the original data into the edited version.

### 14.1 See the code as you edit

Click `Code` in the toolbar to see the code that reproduces your edits so far. The code updates as you edit and can be copied with the `Copy` button. Column actions such as formulas, find and replace, recoding, type changes and sorting (see [Change whole columns](#change-whole-columns)) appear as one `dplyr` verb each; other edits are listed as the values that changed.

```{r, echo = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%"}
screenshot("code.png")
```

When rows are filtered or columns hidden, the code continues with the rows and columns on screen, written as `filter()` and `select()` so that you can take the subset into your script. The filters under the column headers, those from column summaries and those of the `Filters` panel (matching all or any of them) are all included:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
# The rows and columns on screen
mtcars_view <- mtcars %>%
  filter(between(mpg, 15, 25), cyl %in% c(4, 6),
         !grepl("merc", tolower(rownames(.)), fixed = TRUE)) %>%
  select(mpg, cyl, disp, hp)
```

The code is checked by running it on the data before it is shown. When the filters cannot explain the rows on screen (rows added while the data was filtered stay on screen until the filters change), the rows are picked by their position with `slice()` instead, and the code says so.

### 14.2 Print code to console

If you rename the data in the header, the code gives the result the new name, e.g. `cars <- mtcars %>% ...`.

Set `code = TRUE` within `data_edit()` to print the generated code to the console when you press `Done`. The code uses `dplyr` verbs such as `rename()`, `select()`, `mutate()`, `slice()`, and `tibble::add_row()` to replicate your edits. Copying and pasting this code into the console will recreate the edited version of your data. If you return only what's on screen (see [Return or export data subsets](#return-or-export-data-subsets)), the code ends with the `filter()` and `select()` that give those rows and columns.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          code = TRUE)
```

For example, renaming a column, modifying a cell value, removing a row and adding a new row might produce code like:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(dplyr)

mtcars <- mtcars %>%
  tibble::rownames_to_column(var = ".rownames") %>%
  rename(horsepower = hp) %>%
  slice(-5) %>%
  mutate(
    mpg = replace(mpg, 1, 21.5),
    horsepower = replace(horsepower, 3, 95)
  ) %>%
  tibble::add_row(.rownames = "My car", mpg = 26, cyl = NA, disp = NA,
                  horsepower = NA, drat = NA, wt = NA, qsec = NA, vs = NA,
                  am = NA, gear = NA, carb = NA) %>%
  tibble::column_to_rownames(var = ".rownames")
```

For database tables the code uses `rows_update()`, `rows_append()` and `rows_delete()` to make the same changes to the database. If other data is opened from the `Open` menu, the code starts from that data instead (e.g. `iris <- iris %>% ...`), and a new table is created from scratch.

### 14.3 Save code to file

Alternatively, users can get `DataEditR` to automatically create a new R script to store this code by providing a name for the R script to `code`. For example, the below code creates a new R script called `mtcars_edit.R` and inserts the code required to programmatically generate the final edited version of your data.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
data_edit(mtcars,
          code = "mtcars_edit.R")
```

### 14.4 Using `data_code()` directly

The `data_code()` function can also be used outside of `data_edit()` to generate code from any pair of original and edited data frames:

```{r}
library(DataEditR)

# Original data
x <- data.frame(
  A = c(1, 2, 3),
  B = c("x", "y", "z"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Edited data (changed a value and renamed a column)
x_edit <- data.frame(
  A = c(1, 5, 3),
  Beta = c("x", "y", "z"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# Generate code
cat(data_code(x, x_edit, name = "x"))
```

## 15. Shiny modules

The data editor is also available as a shiny module, so you can add an editable table to your own shiny applications with `dataEditUI()` and `dataEditServer()`:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
library(shiny)
library(DataEditR)

ui <- fluidPage(
  dataEditUI("edit")
)

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  edited <- dataEditServer("edit", data = reactive(mtcars))
  observe(print(head(edited())))
}

shinyApp(ui, server)
```

Call `dataEditCommit(edited)` (for example when a *Save* button is pressed) to save the changes: for database tables this writes them to the database, and for other data the current data becomes the new starting point for the review panel. `dataEditChanges(edited)` returns the number of changes that have not been saved yet, e.g. to enable the *Save* button only when there is something to save. See `vignette("shiny-modules", package = "DataEditR")` for the options of the module, saving changes and how it works with the other modules in **DataEditR**.

## Summary

**DataEditR** is a powerful and interactive tool to make your data viewing, entry, filtering and editing as seamless as possible. If you need any help or encounter any issues with **DataEditR** please let me know by posting an issue on [GitHub](https://github.com/DillonHammill/DataEditR/issues).
